recalc_method: OneDrive upload + Excel for the web recalculation on open + File > Create a Copy > Download a Copy readback

canary.method: openpyxl writes formulas with NO cached <v> value, so the uploaded chunk workbooks contain zero cached results. Opening the workbook in Excel for the web from OneDrive recalculates every formula with Microsoft's own web calculation engine; File > Create a Copy > Download a Copy writes those computed values back out as .xlsx. The deterministic canary =1111+2222 in Z1 of EVERY sheet reading back exactly 3333 therefore proves genuine computation -- without recalculation the cell would read back blank (None), since nothing was ever cached. The volatile =NOW() canary is recorded per chunk as corroboration; like the Drive path (and unlike the LibreOffice runner, which converts the same file twice and shows =NOW() differing) a single open yields one timestamp, so now_differs_across_runs is null by design and the deterministic canary is the load-bearing proof. Corroborating this engine specifically: the downloaded package's docProps/app.xml names the application that wrote it, and is recorded verbatim per chunk under app_provenance_per_chunk.

ABS_zero.description: Zero is its own absolute value

ABS_expression_argument.description: Argument can be any expression evaluating to a number

ABS_cell_reference_negative.description: Absolute value of a negative cell reference

ABS_error_propagates.description: Errors in the argument propagate through ABS unchanged rather than being suppressed

FVSCHEDULE_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 unit of principal compounded at 9%, 11% then 10%
FVSCHEDULE_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example (=FVSCHEDULE(1,{0.09,0.11,0.1})) with the result displayed as 1.3309. The documented computation -- principal times the product of (1+rate) over the schedule -- is exact here: 1 * 1.09 * 1.11 * 1.10 = 1.330890 with no rounding, so 1.33089 is asserted at 7 dp rather than the page's 4-dp display

FVSCHEDULE_principal_scaled.description: The schedule is applied multiplicatively to any principal

FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: Excel documents empty cells in the schedule as zeros (a 0% period), not as skipped
FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'The values in schedule can be numbers or blank cells; any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE. Blank cells are taken as zeros (no interest).' So the blank is a 0% period: 1000 * 1.1 * 1.0 * 1.1 = 1210. An engine that silently skipped the blank would get the same answer here, but an engine that errored on the blank would not -- so this pins the documented 'blank means 0%' rule

FVSCHEDULE_negative_rate.description: A negative rate in the schedule shrinks the principal

FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.description: Non-numeric values in the schedule are an error, not a zero
FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE'. Note this is the opposite of most statistical functions, which ignore stray text in a reference, and it differs from an empty cell, which the same sentence documents as a zero rate

LENB_ascii_string.description: Microsoft's documented example string: byte length of an 11-character ASCII string
LENB_ascii_string.notes: Microsoft's LEN/LENB page uses 'Phoenix, AZ' as its worked example and publishes LEN = 11. The DBCS rule (see the LENB_non_ascii_characters case) cannot change the answer here because every character is single-byte under either reading. NOTE: the current live page now states 'The LENB function is deprecated' and has dropped the DBCS explanation entirely

LENB_empty_string.description: An empty string has zero bytes
LENB_empty_string.notes: No characters means no bytes, under either the DBCS or the non-DBCS rule

LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.description: Spaces are characters and are counted, including leading and trailing ones
LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.notes: Microsoft documents 'Spaces count as characters' for the text argument of LEN/LENB; the string here is two spaces, three letters and three spaces = 8

LENB_number_argument_coerced.description: A numeric argument is converted to its text representation before measuring
LENB_number_argument_coerced.notes: The number 1234 becomes the four-character string "1234", so the byte length is 4 in a non-DBCS default language

LENB_non_ascii_characters.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: two CJK characters, where the byte count depends on the DBCS language rule
LENB_non_ascii_characters.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's archived LEN/LENB page: 'LENB counts 2 bytes per character only when a DBCS language is set as the default language. Otherwise LENB behaves the same as LEN, counting 1 byte per character', with DBCS listed as Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional) and Korean. The harness runs under a non-DBCS default locale, so the documented answer is 2 (LEN semantics). An engine that always counts raw UTF-8 or UTF-16 bytes returns 6 or 4 instead -- recording which one each engine does is the point of this case

LENB_propagates_error.description: An error argument propagates instead of being measured
LENB_propagates_error.notes: The argument evaluates to #DIV/0! before LENB sees it, so the error is the result

MIRR_documented_five_years.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 5 years of cash flows, 10% finance rate, 12% reinvestment rate
MIRR_documented_five_years.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 12.61% (the live page displays it rounded to 13%). Independently derived from the documented formula MIRR = (-NPV(reinvest, positives)*(1+reinvest)^n / (NPV(finance, negatives)*(1+finance)))^(1/(n-1)) - 1 with n = 6 values: the reinvested inflows are carried forward at 12% and the single -120000 outflow discounted at 10%; the 5th root of the ratio gives 0.12609413 -> 0.1261 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_first_three_years.description: Same doc example truncated to the first three years of inflows, which is still a net loss
MIRR_documented_first_three_years.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as -4.80% (displayed rounded to -5%). Same formula with n = 4 values (-120000, 39000, 30000, 21000): the reinvested inflows do not recover the outflow, so the cube root of the ratio is below 1 -> -0.04804466 -> -0.048 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.description: Same cash flows with the reinvestment rate raised from 12% to 14%
MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 13.48% (displayed rounded to 13%). Raising only the reinvestment rate raises the future value of the positive flows; recomputing the documented formula gives 0.13475911 -> 0.1348 at 4 dp

MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.description: A zero cash flow is neither an inflow nor an outflow, so it only contributes to the period count
MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.notes: Excel documents that MIRR ignores text, logical values and empty cells in a reference but INCLUDES cells with the value zero. Zero belongs to neither the positive nor the negative NPV; with finance = reinvest = 0.1, the future value of the inflows is 600*1.1 + 700 = 1360 and the compounded present value of the outflow is -1000, with n = 4 values, so (1360/1000)^(1/3) - 1 = 0.10793165 -> 0.1079

MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.description: Excel documents #DIV/0! when values contains no negative (or no positive) number
MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.notes: With no negative cash flow the denominator NPV of the outflows is zero, and Excel documents that MIRR requires at least one positive and one negative value or it returns #DIV/0!

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_example.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,2) = 0.333 for the data 13, 12, 11, 8, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1. DERIVATION in exact rational arithmetic: PERCENTRANK.INC gives the r-th smallest of n values the rank r/(n-1) counting r from 0, so the smallest scores 0 and the largest 1 (the "inclusive" of the name), with linear interpolation for a value not in the data. Microsoft spells the same arithmetic out on the page for its first row: "0.333, because 3 values in the set are smaller than 2, and 6 are larger than 2; 3/(3+6)=0.333". Three of the ten values are below 2, so the rank is 3/9 = 0.3333... and the default three significant digits give 0.333. Microsoft's page was re-read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/percentrank-inc-function (the /en-us/office/<name>-function-<guid> path was serving Microsoft's 'Sorry, the page you're looking for can't be found' body throughout this batch, and the working path returns an 87 KB stub about half the time, so pages were fetched with retries until the payload exceeded 150 KB).

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_truncates_not.description: The documented row whose exact value is 5/9 -- the case that distinguishes truncation from rounding
PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_truncates_not.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,4) = 0.555. THIS IS THE SHARPEST CASE IN THE FILE. Five of the ten values are below 4, so the exact rank is 5/9 = 0.55555... To three significant digits that is 0.555 if the significance argument TRUNCATES and 0.556 if it ROUNDS, and Microsoft publishes 0.555 -- so the documented behaviour is truncation. Microsoft's next row is the same test again in the other direction: =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,8) = 0.666, where 6/9 = 0.6666... truncates to 0.666 and would round to 0.667. An engine that rounds instead of truncating produces a plausible-looking number that differs from Excel in the third decimal on the most ordinary inputs imaginable, and only a case whose exact value is a repeating decimal can see it. EXECUTED RESULT -- A SILENT WRONG ANSWER, AND THE HEADLINE FINDING OF THIS BATCH: LibreOffice returns 0.556 on all four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3), which agree case for case, where Excel documents and publishes 0.555. LibreOffice ROUNDS the result to the significance digits; Excel TRUNCATES it. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the answer is wrong in the third decimal on the most ordinary input imaginable -- a percentile rank of a small integer list. The companion case in this file (rank of 8, exact value 6/9) shows the same split, 0.667 against Microsoft's published 0.666, and PERCENTRANK.EXC's significance-1 row shows it a third time, 0.4 against Microsoft's published 0.3. The corpus's legacy PERCENTRANK file never caught this because every value it asserts is exact at three digits.

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_two_thirds.description: The documented row whose exact value is 6/9
PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_two_thirds.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,8) = 0.666. Six of the ten values are below 8, so the exact rank is 6/9 = 0.66666..., truncated to three significant digits by the default significance: 0.666, not 0.667. Asserted alongside the 5/9 case because the two together make the truncation reading unambiguous -- a single repeating-decimal row could be dismissed as a typo on Microsoft's page, two cannot. EXECUTED RESULT: LibreOffice returns 0.667 on all four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3), which agree case for case, against Microsoft's published 0.666. The second of three demonstrations in this batch that LibreOffice rounds where Excel truncates; see the 5/9 case above.

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_interpolated.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,5) = 0.583 and explains it as "one-quarter of the way between the PERCENTRANK.INC of 4 and the PERCENTRANK.INC of 8". DERIVATION: 5 sits between 4 (rank 5) and 8 (rank 6), a quarter of the way along, so the exact rank is (5 + 1/4)/9 = 21/36 = 0.58333..., truncated to 0.583.

PERCENTRANK.INC_largest_value_is_one.description: The largest member of the array, which the inclusive definition sends to 1
PERCENTRANK.INC_largest_value_is_one.notes: Nine of the ten values are below 13, so the rank is 9/9 = 1 exactly. This is the end of the range where .INC and .EXC part company (.EXC would give 10/11 here), so it pins which of the two definitions the engine implemented.

PERCENTRANK.INC_significance_below_one.description: A significance of zero, which the page excludes
PERCENTRANK.INC_significance_below_one.notes: Microsoft documents: "If significance < 1, PERCENTRANK.INC returns the #NUM! error value."

PERCENTRANK.INC_empty_array.description: An empty array, which the page excludes -- D20:D25 is deliberately left blank
PERCENTRANK.INC_empty_array.notes: Microsoft documents: "If array is empty, PERCENTRANK.INC returns the #NUM! error value." D20:D25 is deliberately empty; nothing is written into it by design.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#N/A'

VAR.P_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten tool readings
VAR.P_documented_population_variance.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 678.84, alongside VAR.S over the same data as 754.27. Independently derived: mean 1328.6, sum of squared deviations 6788.4, divided by n = 10 = 678.84 (VAR.S divides by n-1 and so gives 754.2667)

VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: the paired case to VARPA -- VAR.P IGNORES text rather than counting it as 0
VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.notes: Microsoft's VAR.P page is unambiguous where VARPA's is not: 'Empty cells, logical values, text, or error values in the array or reference are ignored.' Data are 1, 2, 3 with mean 2; squared deviations 1+0+1 = 2, divided by n = 3 gives 0.66667 -> 0.6667. The identical range under VARPA gives 1.25, so the two cases together pin down the coercion rule

VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.description: A logical inside a referenced range is ignored, so only the numbers are used
VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.notes: Microsoft documents logical values in a reference as ignored by VAR.P. Data 4 and 8, mean 6, squared deviations 4+4 = 8, divided by n = 2 gives 4

VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.description: One data point has zero population variance
VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.notes: Population variance divides by n, so a single point gives 0/1 = 0

VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.description: A range holding only text leaves VAR.P with no data points
VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: the VAR.P page documents no error condition. Text in a reference is documented as ignored, so n = 0 and the population denominator is zero -- #DIV/0!

ACCRINT_documented_bond.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: treasury bond issued 2008-03-01, first interest 2008-08-31, settled 2008-05-01, 10% semiannual coupon on 1000 par, US 30/360 basis
ACCRINT_documented_bond.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 16.666667. Independently derived from the documented ACCRINTM-style day-count: serial 39508 = 2008-03-01 (issue), 39569 = 2008-05-01 (settlement), so on the documented US (NASD) 30/360 basis (basis 0) A = (5-3)*30 + (1-1) = 60 accrued days and D = 360, giving par*rate*A/D = 1000*0.1*60/360 = 16.66666667 -> 16.666667 at 6 dp

ACCRINT_documented_calc_false.description: Same terms but issued 2008-03-05, with calc_method FALSE
ACCRINT_documented_calc_false.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 15.555556. Re-derived on the same 30/360 basis: 2008-03-05 to 2008-05-01 is (5-3)*30 + (1-5) = 56 days, so 1000*0.1*56/360 = 15.55555556 -> 15.555556 at 6 dp

ACCRINT_documented_calc_true.description: Same terms but issued 2008-04-05, with calc_method TRUE
ACCRINT_documented_calc_true.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 7.2222222. Re-derived on the same 30/360 basis: 2008-04-05 to 2008-05-01 is (5-4)*30 + (1-5) = 26 days, so 1000*0.1*26/360 = 7.22222222 -> 7.2222222 at 7 dp

ACCRINT_bad_frequency_num.description: A coupon frequency of 3 is not one of the permitted 1, 2 or 4
ACCRINT_bad_frequency_num.notes: Excel documents: "If frequency is any number other than 1, 2, or 4, ACCRINT returns the #NUM! error value."

ACCRINT_zero_rate_num.description: A coupon rate of zero is outside the documented domain
ACCRINT_zero_rate_num.notes: Excel documents: "If rate <= 0 or if par <= 0, ACCRINT returns the #NUM! error value."

ACCRINT_issue_after_settlement_num.description: Issue date later than the settlement date (arguments A2 and A4 swapped)
ACCRINT_issue_after_settlement_num.notes: Excel documents: "If issue >= settlement, ACCRINT returns the #NUM! error value." Here issue = serial 39569 (2008-05-01) and settlement = 39508 (2008-03-01)

ACCRINTM_documented_actual_365.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: issued 2008-04-01, matures 2008-06-15, 10% coupon on 1000 par, Actual/365 basis
ACCRINTM_documented_actual_365.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 20.54794521. Independently derived from the documented formula ACCRINTM = par * rate * A/D: serial 39539 = 2008-04-01 and 39614 = 2008-06-15, so on basis 3 (Actual/365) A = 29 + 31 + 15 = 75 actual days and D = 365, giving 1000*0.1*75/365 = 20.547945205 -> 20.54794521 at 8 dp

ACCRINTM_zero_rate_num.description: A coupon rate of zero is outside the documented domain
ACCRINTM_zero_rate_num.notes: Excel documents: "If rate <= 0 or if par <= 0, ACCRINTM returns the #NUM! error value."

ACCRINTM_basis_out_of_range_num.description: Basis 5 is above the documented 0-4 range
ACCRINTM_basis_out_of_range_num.notes: Excel documents: "If basis < 0 or if basis > 4, ACCRINTM returns the #NUM! error value." The documented basis table stops at 4 (European 30/360)

ACCRINTM_issue_after_settlement_num.description: Issue date later than the maturity date (arguments swapped)
ACCRINTM_issue_after_settlement_num.notes: Excel documents: "If issue >= settlement, ACCRINTM returns the #NUM! error value."

ACOS_documented_radians.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arccosine of -0.5 in radians (2*pi/3)
ACOS_documented_radians.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2.094395102. Independently verified in Python: math.acos(-0.5) = 2.0943951023931957, which is exactly 2*pi/3 -> 2.094395102 at 9 dp

ACOS_documented_degrees.description: The same example converted to degrees, as the documented Remark suggests
ACOS_documented_degrees.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 120. Independently verified: 2*pi/3 radians = 120 degrees exactly; the double-precision product is 120.00000000000001, which is 120 at 9 dp

ACOS_out_of_domain_num.description: An argument above 1 is outside the documented domain
ACOS_out_of_domain_num.notes: Excel documents that number "must be from -1 to 1"; an argument outside the domain of a real-valued math function is Excel's documented #NUM! case ("a formula or function contains invalid numeric values")

ACOS_text_argument_value.notes: The sibling arccosine/arccotangent page for the same function family documents this explicitly ("If Number is a non-numeric value, ACOT returns the #VALUE! error value"); #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type

ACOSH_documented_one.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic cosine of 1
ACOSH_documented_one.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0. Independently verified: cosh(0) = 1, so acosh(1) = 0 exactly (math.acosh(1) = 0.0)

ACOSH_documented_ten.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic cosine of 10
ACOSH_documented_ten.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2.9932228. Independently verified in Python: math.acosh(10) = 2.993222846126381 = ln(10 + sqrt(99)) -> 2.9932228 at 7 dp

ACOSH_below_one_num.description: An argument below 1 is outside the documented domain
ACOSH_below_one_num.notes: Excel documents that number must be "any real number equal to or greater than 1"; below that the inverse hyperbolic cosine is not real, which is Excel's documented #NUM! case

ACOSH_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the ACOT page states it explicitly for this function family

ACOT_documented_two.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arccotangent of 2 in radians
ACOT_documented_two.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.4636. Independently verified: acot(2) = atan(1/2) = 0.4636476090008061 -> 0.4636 at 4 dp. (Excel's ACOT returns the principal value in 0..pi, which for a positive argument agrees with atan(1/x))

ACOT_at_zero_half_pi.description: The arccotangent of zero, the midpoint of the documented 0..pi output range
ACOT_at_zero_half_pi.notes: Excel documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi", and cot(pi/2) = 0, so ACOT(0) = pi/2. Independently verified: math.pi/2 = 1.5707963267948966 -> 1.570796327 at 9 dp. This case distinguishes the documented 0..pi principal branch from the atan(1/x) shortcut, which is undefined at 0

ACOT_negative_argument.description: A negative argument, where the documented 0..pi range differs from atan(1/x)
ACOT_negative_argument.notes: Excel documents the result is in the range 0 to pi, so for a negative argument ACOT(-2) = pi + atan(1/-2) = pi - 0.4636476090008061 = 2.677945044588987 -> 2.677945045 at 9 dp, NOT the negative -0.4636 that atan(1/x) alone would give

ACOT_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If Number is a non-numeric value, ACOT returns the #VALUE! error value."

ACOTH_documented_six.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic cotangent of 6
ACOTH_documented_six.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.168. Independently verified from the documented identity acoth(x) = 0.5*ln((x+1)/(x-1)) = atanh(1/x): atanh(1/6) = 0.16823611831060645 -> 0.168 at 3 dp

ACOTH_negative_argument.description: A negative argument whose absolute value exceeds 1, which the documented domain allows
ACOTH_negative_argument.notes: Excel documents "The absolute value of Number must be greater than 1", so -2 is in the domain. Independently derived from 0.5*ln((x+1)/(x-1)) with x = -2: 0.5*ln(1/3) = -0.5493061443340548 -> -0.549306144 at 9 dp

ACOTH_inside_unit_num.description: An argument whose absolute value is below 1 is outside the documented domain
ACOTH_inside_unit_num.notes: Excel documents: "If Number is less than 1, ACOTH returns the #NUM! error value." (The page's next line repeats the rule for the absolute value but misnames the function as ACOT and misnames the error as #VALUE!; the #NUM! statement is the one that names ACOTH, and 0.5 satisfies both stated conditions)

ACOTH_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the companion ACOT page states it explicitly for this function family

ADD_documented_sample_literals.description: The page's own Sample Usage line on literal arguments
ADD_documented_sample_literals.notes: Google's Sample Usage prints the formula ADD(3,4) AND NOTHING ELSE -- there is no result column on this page, so 7 is DERIVED, not quoted, from the page's one-line definition: "Returns the sum of two numbers. Equivalent to the `+` operator." Google's ADD page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093590. BATCH PROVENANCE (batch H, the first Sheets/LibreOffice-only batch). Every function in this batch has x == false in docs/data/compat.json: it is a Google Sheets function that Microsoft does not document at all, so this corpus makes NO claim about it in that engine and nothing here is measured against that vendor's documentation. The authority is Google's own support.google.com function page, cited by full URL and by the date it was read -- Google publishes no version number for these pages, so a bare URL dates nothing. WHAT GOOGLE ACTUALLY PRINTS, WHICH IS LESS THAN IT LOOKS: most of these pages carry a 'Sample Usage' block of FORMULAS WITH NO RESULTS. Where a value below is Google's own published output the note says so; where it is derived from the page's stated semantics the note says that instead, and says from which sentence. No value in this batch was taken from a search snippet, a blog or a mirror. AI_generative_prompt_probe.notes: NOT ASSERTABLE BY DESIGN, and deliberately recorded as a probe (expected: null) rather than a support claim -- the treatment batch B gave the CUBE* family and COPILOT, batch C gave DETECTLANGUAGE, and batch G gave RTD, STOCKHISTORY and TRANSLATE. Google's page publishes the syntax `AI("prompt",[optional range])` and the example `=AI("Generate slogan for event in 10 words or less", A2)`, which is the formula this case runs verbatim. THE VALUE IS GENERATED TEXT, NOT A COMPUTED FUNCTION OF THE ARGUMENTS. Google gates the feature -- "This feature requires an eligible Google Workspace or Google AI plan." -- and rations it -- "The AI function has short term and long term generation limits." -- and the page's own capability list includes "Access real-time information from Google Search", so an answer may depend on the live web at the moment of evaluation. WHAT GOOGLE DOES NOT SAY, SAID PLAINLY: this page carries no sentence promising that the output varies between runs, so no determinism disclaimer is attributed to Google here. The unassertability is INFERRED from the generative framing and the real-time-search capability quoted above, and is labelled as inference rather than dressed up as documentation. LIBREOFFICE, MEASURED BEFORE THIS FILE WAS AUTHORED. All four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) were probed with NINE storage spellings -- plain, _xlfn., COM.MICROSOFT., ORG.OPENOFFICE., _xlfn.ORG.OPENOFFICE., ORG.LIBREOFFICE., _xlfn.ORG.LIBREOFFICE., _xlfn.COM.MICROSOFT. and COM.SUN.STAR.SHEET.ADDIN.ANALYSIS. -- and every one of those 36 combinations returned #NAME?. LibreOffice's own parser additionally wrote the name back into the converted file LOWER-CASED ('=ai("Say hello")'), which is what it does with an identifier it does not recognise as a function at all rather than with a function it knows under a different storage token. A #NAME? under all nine storage forms on all four builds is therefore a genuine absence and not a storage-form artifact of this harness, which is why 'unsupported in LibreOffice' IS a verdict this file publishes even though the returned VALUE is not assertable in any engine. BATCH PROVENANCE (batch J, group B of sheets-lo-only-plan.md -- Google-documented, service- or context-bound; the final batch of the completeness push). This function has x == false in docs/data/compat.json: Microsoft does not document it at all, so this corpus makes no claim about Excel, nothing here is measured against Microsoft's documentation, and the Excel column on the published page reads 'n/a (not an Excel function)' rather than a verdict. The authority is Google's own function help, cited by full URL and by the date it was read (2026-08-31) -- Google publishes no version number for Sheets, so a bare URL dates nothing. GOOGLE SHEETS: this batch builds the Sheets chunk whose ingest will record what the service returns for this call. Until that ingest lands the Sheets column on the published page reads 'Not yet' and nothing in this file claims anything about it. (Stated positively on purpose -- scripts/check_honesty.py bans the blanket negative shape of that sentence, and the guard is worth keeping blunt.) Google's AI function help page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/15877199.

AMORDEGRC_documented_period_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 2400 asset bought 2008-08-19, first period ends 2008-12-31, salvage 300, period 1, 15% rate, actual basis
AMORDEGRC_documented_period_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 776. Independently derived from the documented depreciation-coefficient rule: life = 1/rate = 6.667 years, which is "More than 6 years", so the documented coefficient is 2.5 and the effective rate is 0.15*2.5 = 0.375. Serial 39679 = 2008-08-19 and 39813 = 2008-12-31, so on basis 1 (actual) the prorated first period is 134/366 of a year (2008 is a leap year) and period 0 depreciates ROUND(2400*0.375*134/366) = ROUND(329.508) = 330. Period 1 then depreciates ROUND((2400-330)*0.375) = ROUND(776.25) = 776, reproducing the published figure exactly

AMORDEGRC_period_0_prorated.description: The prorated period-0 depreciation implied by the documented example's own arithmetic
AMORDEGRC_period_0_prorated.notes: Not published directly by Microsoft, but forced by the published period-1 figure: 776 = ROUND((2400 - period0)*0.375) has period0 = 330 as its only integer solution consistent with the documented mid-period proration ROUND(cost * rate * coefficient * days/year) = ROUND(2400*0.375*134/366) = ROUND(329.508) = 330. Verified in Python

AMORDEGRC_life_between_4_and_5_num.description: A 22% rate gives a 4.55-year asset life, which the documentation excludes
AMORDEGRC_life_between_4_and_5_num.notes: Excel documents: "If the life of assets is between 0 (zero) and 1, 1 and 2, 2 and 3, or 4 and 5, the #NUM! error value is returned." Here 1/0.22 = 4.545 years falls in the excluded 4-to-5 band (the documented coefficient table only covers 3-4, 5-6 and >6); MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got 886

AMORLINC_documented_verbatim.description: Microsoft's documented worked example, transcribed verbatim including the page's own repeated A7 in the basis position
AMORLINC_documented_verbatim.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 360. The published formula passes A7 (0.15) rather than A8 (1) as basis -- an apparent typo on the page -- but a basis of 0.15 truncates to 0 (US 30/360) and the answer is unaffected, because AMORLINC depreciates a full accounting period linearly at cost*rate: 2400*0.15 = 360, with no day-count proration for period 1. Verified in Python; the basis only affects the prorated period 0

AMORLINC_documented_basis_fixed.description: The same example with the basis argument corrected to A8 (actual basis), as the page's data table intends
AMORLINC_documented_basis_fixed.notes: Same documented result of 360. A full (non-prorated) accounting period depreciates cost*rate = 2400*0.15 = 360 under the documented linear method regardless of day-count basis, so correcting the page's A7/A8 typo must not change the answer -- this case and the verbatim one above are a paired check of exactly that

AMORLINC_second_full_period.description: The second full accounting period of the same asset
AMORLINC_second_full_period.notes: Excel documents AMORLINC as straight-line depreciation with only the first (purchase) period prorated, so every subsequent full period depreciates the same cost*rate = 2400*0.15 = 360. Independently checked that period 2 is not near the end of the asset's life: accumulated depreciation through period 2 is about 131.8 + 360 + 360 = 851.8, well under cost - salvage = 2100, so no salvage clamping applies

AMORLINC_higher_rate_full_period.description: The same asset at a 25% rate, checking the linear cost*rate relationship directly
AMORLINC_higher_rate_full_period.notes: Derived from the documented straight-line method: a full period depreciates cost*rate = 2400*0.25 = 600. Accumulated depreciation through period 1 is about 219.7 + 600 = 819.7, under cost - salvage = 2100, so no salvage clamping applies

POST-EXECUTION ADDENDUM -- THE ONLY CROSS-BUILD DIFFERENCE IN THIS BATCH, AND IT IS ABOUT AN ERROR CODE, NOT A VALUE. This case returns #NAME? on 24.2.0.3 but #VALUE! on 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3 and 25.8.7.3. ARRAY_CONSTRAIN is absent from all four builds under all five storage spellings, so the difference is not about ARRAY_CONSTRAIN at all -- it is about the nested SORT. The harness stores SORT as _xlfn._xlws.SORT; 24.2 does not implement it, so the whole expression fails to resolve a name and the result is #NAME?, while on the three later builds SORT resolves and LibreOffice reports the still-unrecognised OUTER name as #VALUE! instead. LibreOffice's error code for an unknown function is therefore not stable: it depends on whether that function's ARGUMENTS resolved. Every other ARRAY_CONSTRAIN case in this file is #NAME? on all four builds, which is what the published verdict rests on.; MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 28, got '#NAME?'

ASC_halfwidth_unchanged.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: text with no full-width characters is returned unchanged
ASC_halfwidth_unchanged.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example verbatim: '=ASC("EXCEL") equals "EXCEL"'. The documentation adds "If text does not contain any full-width letters, text is not changed"

ASC_fullwidth_latin_to_halfwidth.description: Full-width (double-byte) Latin letters converted to half-width
ASC_fullwidth_latin_to_halfwidth.notes: The page's second example is the same word in full-width characters, but it is rendered as inline images so the literal argument cannot be copied from the page; this case reconstructs it from the documented rule that the function "changes full-width (double-byte) characters to half-width (single-byte) characters". The argument is U+FF25 U+FF38 U+FF23 U+FF25 U+FF2C (FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL E X C E L), whose documented half-width forms are the ASCII letters EXCEL; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'EXCEL', got 'ＥＸＣＥＬ'

ASC_fullwidth_digits_and_space.description: Full-width letter, full-width digits and an ideographic space
ASC_fullwidth_digits_and_space.notes: Derived from the same documented full-width-to-half-width rule: U+FF21 -> A, U+FF11/FF12/FF13 -> 1/2/3, and U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE -> U+0020 half-width space, giving the five-character string "A123 " (trailing half-width space); MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'A123 ', got 'Ａ１２３\u3000'

ASC_length_preserved.description: The conversion is character-for-character, so the length is unchanged
ASC_length_preserved.notes: Excel documents ASC as changing full-width characters to half-width characters, a one-for-one character mapping rather than an encoding change, so a five-character input yields a five-character result. This case separates a genuine width conversion from a byte-level reinterpretation

ASIN_documented_degrees.description: The same example converted to degrees, as the documented Remark suggests
ASIN_documented_degrees.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -30. Independently verified: -pi/6 radians = -30 degrees exactly; the double-precision product is -30.000000000000004, which is -30 at 9 dp

ASINH_documented_ten.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic sine of 10

ATAN2_documented_first_quadrant.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (1,1), which is pi/4

ATAN2_documented_third_quadrant.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (-1,-1), which is -3*pi/4

AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_two_pairs_fro.description: Published example-table row 1: two values and two weights taken from ranges
AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_two_pairs_fro.notes: GOOGLE'S OWN PUBLISHED RESULT, from the Formula/Result table in the article body: =AVERAGE.WEIGHTED(A1:A2, B1:B2) -> 3.5, over the table's own data (A1=2, A2=4, A3=8, B1=1, B2=3, B3=6). Derived independently as (2*1 + 4*3)/(1+3) = 14/4 = 3.5. Google's AVERAGE.WEIGHTED page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9084098. BATCH PROVENANCE (batch H, the first Sheets/LibreOffice-only batch). Every function in this batch has x == false in docs/data/compat.json: it is a Google Sheets function that Microsoft does not document at all, so this corpus makes NO claim about it in that engine and nothing here is measured against that vendor's documentation. The authority is Google's own support.google.com function page, cited by full URL and by the date it was read -- Google publishes no version number for these pages, so a bare URL dates nothing. WHAT GOOGLE ACTUALLY PRINTS, WHICH IS LESS THAN IT LOOKS: most of these pages carry a 'Sample Usage' block of FORMULAS WITH NO RESULTS. Where a value below is Google's own published output the note says so; where it is derived from the page's stated semantics the note says that instead, and says from which sentence. No value in this batch was taken from a search snippet, a blog or a mirror. LIBREOFFICE: probed on all four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) in five storage spellings -- plain, _xlfn., COM.MICROSOFT., ORG.OPENOFFICE. and _xlfn.ORG.OPENOFFICE. -- and #NAME? under every one of them, so the expected values below describe Google Sheets and the LibreOffice column records absence.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 3.5, got '#NAME?'

AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_inline_values.description: Published row 2: values and weights given inline rather than as ranges
AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_inline_values.notes: GOOGLE'S OWN PUBLISHED RESULT: =AVERAGE.WEIGHTED(2, 10, 4, 15) -> 3.2. Derived independently as (2*10 + 4*15)/(10+15) = 80/25 = 3.2. This row is what fixes the ARGUMENT ORDER as value, weight, value, weight -- the syntax line alone (values, weights, [additional values], [additional weights]) could be read the other way. Google's AVERAGE.WEIGHTED page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9084098.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 3.2, got '#NAME?'

AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_row_3_with_co.description: Published row 3's result, with the cell references its own table contradicts
AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_row_3_with_co.notes: THE PUBLISHED FORMULA IN THIS ROW CANNOT PRODUCE THE PUBLISHED ANSWER, AND THE PAGE'S OWN LAYOUT SHOWS WHY. Google prints "=AVERAGE.WEIGHTED(A1:A2, B1:B2, C1, C2)" -> 6.2. But in that same example table column C is the FORMULA column and column D the RESULT column: C1 holds the header word "Formula" and C2 holds the first example formula. A weighted average cannot take a header string as an additional value and another formula as its weight. The data the row must have meant is the third row of the table's own data block, A3=8 and B3=6, and that reproduces the published figure exactly: (2*1 + 4*3 + 8*6)/(1+3+6) = 62/10 = 6.2. This case therefore asserts Google's published RESULT through the references its data requires, and records the printed references as wrong. Google's AVERAGE.WEIGHTED page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9084098.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 6.2, got '#NAME?'

AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_course_grade_.description: Published second example: a course grade weighted by percentage of final grade
AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_published_course_grade_.notes: GOOGLE'S OWN PUBLISHED RESULT from the page's second example table: =AVERAGE.WEIGHTED(B2:B6, C2:C6) -> 87.7, over grades 95/90/85/88/82 weighted 25%/10%/15%/20%/30%. Derived independently as 23.75 + 9 + 12.75 + 17.6 + 24.6 = 87.7. The percentages are stored here as the numbers 0.25 ... 0.3, which is what a cell displaying "25%" contains. This is the only published example whose weights sum to exactly 1. Google's AVERAGE.WEIGHTED page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9084098.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 87.7, got '#NAME?'

AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_zero_weight_is_allowed.description: A zero weight, which the argument description explicitly permits
AVERAGE.WEIGHTED_zero_weight_is_allowed.notes: DERIVED from the `weights` argument description: "Weights cannot be negative, though they can be zero. At least one of the weights must be positive." A zero weight must therefore drop its value out of both the numerator and the denominator: (2*1 + 4*0 + 8*1)/(1+0+1) = 10/2 = 5. Google publishes no example with a zero weight and names NO error value for a negative weight, so this corpus asserts nothing about negative weights. Google's AVERAGE.WEIGHTED page, read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9084098.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 5, got '#NAME?'

AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.description: Microsoft's documented example: four numbers plus a text cell, where the text is averaged in as 0
AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 5.6 and explains it as 'The cell with the text "Not available" is used in the calculation', i.e. (10+7+9+2+0)/5. The text cell contributes a 0 AND is counted in the divisor, which is exactly how AVERAGEA differs from AVERAGE (AVERAGE would give 28/4 = 7). This worked example is what resolves the same text-vs-ignored contradiction that appears on the MAXA, MINA and VARPA pages

AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: TRUE is counted as 1 and FALSE as 0, both counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.notes: Excel documents TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 for AVERAGEA: (1+1+0)/3 = 0.666666... -> 0.6667 at 4 dp. An engine using AVERAGE semantics (logicals in ranges ignored) would return 1

AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Empty cells are ignored entirely -- not counted as 0 and not counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Microsoft's second worked example on the same page averages a range plus a separate cell and still returns 5.6 because the empty cell is not counted. Empty cells are ignored by AVERAGEA (only text and logicals are coerced), so the answer here is (10+20)/2 = 15, not (10+0+20)/3

AVERAGEA_all_text_range.description: A range containing only text averages the coerced zeros rather than erroring
AVERAGEA_all_text_range.notes: Under the documented 'array or reference arguments that contain text evaluate as 0' rule both cells count as 0 and both count in the divisor: (0+0)/2 = 0. Microsoft's page also states explicitly that empty text ("") evaluates as 0

AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.description: A range of only empty cells has no data points at all
AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's AVERAGEA page documents no error condition. But it does document that empty cells are ignored, so a range of only empty cells leaves no data points and the average's divisor is zero -- #DIV/0! is the only consistent result

AVERAGEIF_basic.description: Average of cells in the range itself that satisfy the criteria

AVERAGEIF_separate_average_range.description: Criteria evaluated against A but matching B cells are averaged
AVERAGEIF_separate_average_range.notes: Rows 3,4,5 satisfy A>2; average of paired B = (30+40+50)/3

AVERAGEIF_no_match_div0.description: No cells satisfy the criteria -> #DIV/0! per Microsoft docs (same as AVERAGE of an empty set)

AVERAGEIF_blank_average_range_cells_excl.description: Blank cells in average_range are excluded from both the sum and the count, not treated as 0
AVERAGEIF_blank_average_range_cells_excl.notes: A1:A3 all satisfy >0, but B2 is blank; average is (10+30)/2=20, not (10+0+30)/3

AVERAGEIFS_basic.description: Average of A where paired B > 2

AVERAGEIFS_multi_criteria.notes: Only rows 2,3 satisfy B>1 AND C<5; average of 20,30 = 25

AVERAGEIFS_wildcard.notes: apple and avocado match a*; average of 10,30 = 20

BAHTTEXT_documented_1234.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 1234 rendered as Thai text with a Baht suffix
BAHTTEXT_documented_1234.value: หนึ่งพันสองร้อยสามสิบสี่บาทถ้วน
BAHTTEXT_documented_1234.expected: หนึ่งพันสองร้อยสามสิบสี่บาทถ้วน
BAHTTEXT_documented_1234.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the Thai string for "one thousand two hundred thirty four Baht", transcribed here character for character from the page: หนึ่ง (one) พัน (thousand) สอง (two) ร้อย (hundred) สาม (three) สิบ (ten) สี่ (four) บาท (Baht) ถ้วน (exactly). The documented output is a 31-character Thai string

BAHTTEXT_returns_text.description: The result is a text value, not a number
BAHTTEXT_returns_text.notes: Excel documents BAHTTEXT as converting "a number to Thai text", so the result is a text value and ISTEXT is TRUE. This case survives any locale-dependent difference in the Baht wording, unlike the exact-string case above

BAHTTEXT_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents the single argument as "A number you want to convert to text, or a reference to a cell containing a number, or a formula that evaluates to a number"; non-numeric text is the wrong argument type, which is Excel's documented #VALUE! case

BESSELI_documented_1_5_order_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: modified Bessel function I at x=1.5, order 1
BESSELI_documented_1_5_order_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.981666428. Independently re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besseli(1, 1.5) = 0.98166642857790758565, so the true value rounds to 0.981666429 at 9 dp -- the page's trailing 8 is a TRUNCATION of ...4285 rather than a round. Asserting at 8 dp (0.98166643) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the true value agree, so a mismatch here is an engine difference and not a documentation artefact

BESSELI_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELI_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 1.9 must behave exactly as order 1 and return the same 0.98166643 as the documented example above. Independently verified with mpmath: besseli(1, 1.5) = 0.9816664285779076; besseli(1.9, 1.5) would be 0.38286062, so this case distinguishes truncation from a real fractional-order evaluation

BESSELI_negative_order_num.notes: Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELI returns the #NUM! error value."

BESSELI_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELI returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELJ_documented_1_9_order_2.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: Bessel function J at x=1.9, order 2
BESSELJ_documented_1_9_order_2.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.329925829, but that figure is WRONG in the 7th decimal place. Re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.32992572769238721660 (scipy.special.jv agrees to machine precision), which differs from the published 0.329925829 by 1.01e-07 -- far larger than the ~1e-10 rounding residue seen on the sibling BESSELY page. Asserting at 6 dp (0.329926) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the mathematically correct value still agree, so this case tests the function rather than Microsoft's typo

BESSELJ_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELJ_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 2.7 must behave exactly as order 2. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.3299257276923872, while a genuine fractional-order besselj(2.7, 1.9) would be about 0.16248, so this case separates truncation from fractional-order evaluation

BESSELJ_zero_order_at_zero.description: The order-0 Bessel function at the origin
BESSELJ_zero_order_at_zero.notes: Follows from the documented series definition on the page: J_0(0) is the k=0 term (-1)^0/(0! * Gamma(1)) * (0/2)^0 = 1, with every later term carrying a positive power of x/2 and vanishing. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(0, 0) = 1.0 exactly; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 1.0, got 1.000000003

BESSELJ_negative_order_num.notes: Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELJ returns the #NUM! error value."

BESSELJ_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELJ returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELK_documented_1_5_order_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: modified Bessel function K at x=1.5, order 1
BESSELK_documented_1_5_order_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.277387804. Independently re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besselk(1, 1.5) = 0.27738780045684381609, so the correct 9-dp value is 0.277387800 and the page's trailing ...804 is off by 3.5e-09. Asserting at 8 dp (0.2773878) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the true value agree

BESSELK_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELK_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 1.4 must behave exactly as order 1 and return the documented 0.2773878. Independently verified with mpmath: a genuine fractional-order besselk(1.4, 1.5) would be about 0.35394, so this case separates truncation from fractional-order evaluation

BESSELK_negative_order_num.notes: Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELK returns the #NUM! error value."

BESSELK_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELK returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELY_documented_2_5_order_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: Weber (Neumann) Bessel function Y at x=2.5, order 1
BESSELY_documented_2_5_order_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.145918138. Independently re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: bessely(1, 2.5) = 0.14591813796678579888 -> 0.145918138 at 9 dp, an exact match (unlike the sibling BESSELI/BESSELJ/BESSELK pages, whose published last digits are truncated or wrong)

BESSELY_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELY_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 1.6 must behave exactly as order 1. Independently verified with mpmath: a genuine fractional-order bessely(1.6, 2.5) would be about -0.19313, so this case separates truncation from fractional-order evaluation

BESSELY_negative_order_num.notes: Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELY returns the #NUM! error value."

BESSELY_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELY returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETA.DIST_doc_cumulative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: cumulative beta distribution at x=2 with alpha=8, beta=10 on the interval [1,3]
BETA.DIST_doc_cumulative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.6854706. Independently derived from the documented definition (the beta CDF rescaled to [A,B]): I_{(x-A)/(B-A)}(alpha,beta) = I_{0.5}(8,10), the regularized incomplete beta function, which scipy.special.betainc(8,10,0.5) gives as 0.6854705810546875 -> 0.6854706 at 7 dp

BETA.DIST_doc_density.description: The same parameters with cumulative FALSE, returning the probability density
BETA.DIST_doc_density.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 1.4837646. Independently derived from the beta density rescaled to [A,B]: f((x-A)/(B-A); 8,10)/(B-A) = beta.pdf(0.5,8,10)/2 = 2.967529296875/2 = 1.4837646484374996 -> 1.4837646 at 7 dp

BETA.DIST_standard_interval.description: The same distribution on the default interval, with A and B omitted
BETA.DIST_standard_interval.notes: Excel documents "If you omit values for A and B, BETA.DIST uses the standard cumulative beta distribution, so that A = 0 and B = 1". Because x=2 on [1,3] rescales to exactly 0.5 on [0,1], this must return the identical 0.6854706 as the documented example -- a direct check of the documented default-bounds rule

BETA.DIST_alpha_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETA.DIST returns the #NUM! error value."

BETA.DIST_x_above_upper_num.description: An x value above the upper bound B
BETA.DIST_x_above_upper_num.notes: Excel documents: "If x < A, x > B, or A = B, BETA.DIST returns the #NUM! error value." Here x = 4 exceeds B = 3

BETA.DIST_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETA.DIST returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETA.INV_doc_roundtrip.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the inverse of the cumulative beta distribution at probability 0.685470581, alpha=8, beta=10 on [1,3]
BETA.INV_doc_roundtrip.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2. Independently derived from the documented inverse relationship ("BETA.INV seeks that value x such that BETA.DIST(x, alpha, beta, TRUE, A, B) = probability"): A + (B-A)*betaincinv(8,10,0.685470581) = 1 + 2*0.4999999999815714 = 1.9999999999631428 -> 2 at 6 dp. The tiny shortfall comes from the input probability itself being the 9-dp rounding of BETA.DIST(2,8,10,TRUE,1,3), so 6 dp is the honest assertion depth

BETA.INV_standard_median.description: The median of a Beta(2,3) distribution on the default [0,1] interval
BETA.INV_standard_median.notes: Excel documents that omitting A and B uses the standard beta distribution on [0,1]. Independently derived: scipy.special.betaincinv(2,3,0.5) = 0.3857275681323895 -> 0.3857276 at 7 dp

BETA.INV_probability_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If probability <= 0 or probability > 1, BETA.INV returns the #NUM! error value." Note the asymmetry -- probability = 1 is allowed but probability = 0 is not

BETA.INV_probability_above_one_num.notes: Excel documents the same rule for probability > 1

BETA.INV_beta_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETA.INV returns the #NUM! error value."

BETA.INV_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETA.INV returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETADIST_doc_cumulative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example for the legacy (pre-2010) name: cumulative beta distribution at x=2, alpha=8, beta=10 on [1,3]
BETADIST_doc_cumulative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.6854706, the same figure as the modern BETA.DIST page. Independently derived from the regularized incomplete beta function: scipy.special.betainc(8,10,(2-1)/(3-1)) = betainc(8,10,0.5) = 0.6854705810546875 -> 0.6854706 at 7 dp. BETADIST has no `cumulative` argument -- it is always the CDF

BETADIST_standard_interval.description: The same distribution on the default interval, with A and B omitted
BETADIST_standard_interval.notes: Excel documents "If you omit values for A and B, BETADIST uses the standard cumulative beta distribution, so that A = 0 and B = 1", and x=2 on [1,3] rescales to exactly 0.5 on [0,1], so the result must be identical to the documented example

BETADIST_beta_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETADIST returns the #NUM! error value."

BETADIST_x_below_lower_num.description: An x value below the lower bound A
BETADIST_x_below_lower_num.notes: Excel documents: "If x < A, x > B, or A = B, BETADIST returns the #NUM! error value." Here x = 0 is below A = 1

BETADIST_equal_bounds_num.notes: Excel documents the same rule for the degenerate case A = B, where the rescaling (x-A)/(B-A) would divide by zero -- note the documented error is #NUM!, not #DIV/0!

BETADIST_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETADIST returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETAINV_doc_roundtrip.description: Microsoft's documented worked example for the legacy (pre-2010) name: the inverse cumulative beta distribution at probability 0.685470581, alpha=8, beta=10 on [1,3]
BETAINV_doc_roundtrip.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2. Independently derived from the documented inverse relationship: A + (B-A)*betaincinv(8,10,0.685470581) = 1 + 2*0.4999999999815714 = 1.9999999999631428 -> 2 at 6 dp; the residue comes from the input probability being a 9-dp rounding of BETADIST(2,8,10,1,3)

BETAINV_standard_median.description: The median of a Beta(8,10) distribution on the default [0,1] interval
BETAINV_standard_median.notes: Excel documents that omitting A and B uses the standard beta distribution on [0,1]. Independently derived: scipy.special.betaincinv(8,10,0.5) = 0.44234231838132165 -> 0.4423423 at 7 dp

BETAINV_probability_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If probability <= 0 or probability > 1, BETAINV returns the #NUM! error value."

BETAINV_alpha_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETAINV returns the #NUM! error value."

BETAINV_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETAINV returns the #VALUE! error value."

BIN2DEC_basic.description: Converts a binary value to its decimal number

BIN2DEC_roundtrip.description: BIN2DEC reverses DEC2BIN, recovering the original number

BIN2HEX_padded.description: The optional places argument pads the hex result to a fixed width

BIN2OCT_padded.description: The optional places argument pads the octal result to a fixed width

BINOM.DIST_doc_pmf.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: probability of exactly 6 successes in 10 trials at p=0.5
BINOM.DIST_doc_pmf.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.2050781. Independently derived from the documented probability mass function COMBIN(n,x)*p^x*(1-p)^(n-x): C(10,6)*0.5^10 = 210/1024 = 0.205078125 exactly -> 0.2050781 at 7 dp

BINOM.DIST_cumulative.description: The same parameters with cumulative TRUE, giving the probability of at most 6 successes
BINOM.DIST_cumulative.notes: Excel documents that with cumulative TRUE the function returns "the probability that there are at most number_s successes", i.e. the sum of the mass function for k = 0..6. Independently derived: (C(10,0)+...+C(10,6))/1024 = (1+10+45+120+210+252+210)/1024 = 848/1024 = 0.828125 exactly

BINOM.DIST_trials_truncated.description: Non-integer number_s and trials, which the documentation says are truncated
BINOM.DIST_trials_truncated.notes: Excel documents "Number_s and trials are truncated to integers", so 6.9 and 10.9 must behave exactly as 6 and 10 and return the documented 0.205078125. Independently checked that a genuine non-truncating evaluation would differ: with 7 successes in 11 trials the mass is C(11,7)*0.5^11 = 330/2048 = 0.161133

BINOM.DIST_successes_above_trials_num.notes: Excel documents: "If number_s < 0 or number_s > trials, BINOM.DIST returns the #NUM! error value."

BINOM.DIST_probability_above_one_num.notes: Excel documents: "If probability_s < 0 or probability_s > 1, BINOM.DIST returns the #NUM! error value."

BINOM.DIST_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If number_s, trials, or probability_s is nonnumeric, BINOM.DIST returns the #VALUE! error value."

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_single.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: probability of exactly 48 successes in 60 trials at p=0.75
BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_single.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.084 (8.4%). Independently derived from the documented summation with s2 omitted (so the sum has the single term k=48): C(60,48)*0.75^48*0.25^12 = 0.0839749674290475 -> 0.084 at 3 dp

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_range.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: probability of between 45 and 50 successes inclusive
BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_range.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.524 (52.4%). Independently derived by summing the binomial mass over k = 45..50 inclusive (the documented equation sums from s to s2): 0.5236297934718872 -> 0.524 at 3 dp. This case also pins the INCLUSIVE upper bound: excluding k=50 would give 0.482911

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_single_6dp.description: The same single-value example asserted at full precision rather than the page's 3 dp
BINOM.DIST.RANGE_single_6dp.notes: Microsoft rounds this example to 0.084 on the page. Re-derived exactly from the documented equation: C(60,48)*0.75^48*0.25^12 = 0.0839749674290475 -> 0.083975 at 6 dp. Asserting at 6 dp catches an engine that agrees to the published 3 dp but computes the tail differently

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_successes_above_trials_.notes: Excel documents that Number_s "must be greater than or equal to 0 and less than or equal to Trials" and that "If any arguments are outside of their constraints, BINOM.DIST.RANGE returns the #NUM! error value"

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_probability_above_one_n.notes: Excel documents that Probability_s "must be greater than or equal to 0 and less than or equal to 1", with #NUM! for arguments outside their constraints

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any arguments are non-numeric values, BINOM.DIST.RANGE returns the #VALUE! error value."

BINOM.INV_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: smallest k with cumulative binomial >= 0.75 for 6 trials at p=0.5
BINOM.INV_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 4. Independently derived by tabulating the cumulative binomial for n=6, p=0.5: k=0 -> 0.015625, k=1 -> 0.109375, k=2 -> 0.34375, k=3 -> 0.65625, k=4 -> 0.890625. The first k whose cumulative probability reaches the 0.75 criterion is 4

BINOM.INV_criterion_at_boundary.description: A criterion value exactly equal to a cumulative probability, testing the documented >= comparison
BINOM.INV_criterion_at_boundary.notes: Excel documents "the smallest value for which the cumulative binomial distribution is greater than or equal to a criterion value". The cumulative probability at k=3 is exactly 42/64 = 0.65625, so a >= comparison returns 3 while a strict > comparison would return 4 -- this case separates the two

BINOM.INV_trials_truncated.description: A non-integer trials argument, which the documentation says is truncated
BINOM.INV_trials_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If trials is not an integer, it is truncated", so 6.9 must behave as 6 and return the documented 4. Independently checked that this discriminates: with n=7 the cumulative reaches 0.75 first at k=4 as well, but the underlying distribution differs, so this case is paired with the doc example rather than standing alone

BITXOR_basic.description: Bitwise XOR of 110 and 011 sets bits present in exactly one: 101 = 5

BITXOR_self_cancels.description: XORing a value with itself clears every bit to 0

CEILING_basic.description: Basic case, rounds 2.5 up to the nearest multiple of 1. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f (worked example table)

CEILING_fractional_significance.description: Rounds 0.234 up to the nearest multiple of 0.01. Source: Microsoft CEILING docs worked example table.

CEILING_both_negative_away_from_zero.description: Number and significance both negative -> rounds away from zero (more negative), per Microsoft's documented rule and worked example.
CEILING_both_negative_away_from_zero.notes: Microsoft: 'If number is negative, and significance is negative, the value is rounded down, away from zero.' Worked example CEILING(-2.5,-2)=-4 at https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f

CEILING_negative_number_positive_signifi.description: Number negative, significance positive -> rounds up toward zero (less negative), per Microsoft's documented rule and worked example.
CEILING_negative_number_positive_signifi.notes: Microsoft: 'If number is negative, and significance is positive, the value is rounded up towards zero.' Worked example CEILING(-2.5,2)=-2 at the same doc page.

CEILING_libreoffice_default_mode_diverge.description: GOLD QUIRK CANDIDATE: identical 2-argument call (Mode omitted) with number and significance both negative. Per Microsoft's documented CEILING rule this must round AWAY from zero.
CEILING_libreoffice_default_mode_diverge.notes: Microsoft (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f): both-negative case rounds away from zero, so CEILING(-45.67,-2) -> -46 (ratio -45.67/-2=22.835, ceiling(22.835)=23, 23*-2=-46). LibreOffice's own CEILING docs (https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/scalc/01/func_ceiling.html) define a 3rd optional Mode argument that ONLY applies when both Number and Significance are negative, and state: 'if Mode is equal to zero or not given, negative numbers are rounded up (towards zero)' -- with LO's own worked example CEILING(-45.67;-2;0) = -44. That means the identical 2-arg formula (Mode omitted) is documented to resolve to -44 under LibreOffice's own default, vs -46 under Microsoft's documented default -- a genuine cross-engine default-behavior divergence for the exact same formula text, not just a wording difference. If LO's executed result is -44, matched_expected:false here is the intended, correct signal of that divergence -- do not 'fix' this expectation to match LO.

CEILING_nonnumeric_error.description: Nonnumeric first argument -> #VALUE!, per Microsoft docs: 'If either argument is nonnumeric, CEILING returns the #VALUE! error value.'

CEILING.MATH_basic_significance.description: Rounds 24.3 up to the nearest multiple of 5. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-math-function-80f95d2f-b499-4eee-9f16-f795a8e306c8 (worked example table)

CEILING.MATH_default_significance_1.description: Significance and mode both omitted -> defaults to nearest integer (significance 1). Source: Microsoft CEILING.MATH docs.

CEILING.MATH_negative_default_mode_towar.description: Negative number, mode omitted -> unlike the modeless legacy CEILING function, CEILING.MATH's default for negative numbers rounds TOWARD zero.
CEILING.MATH_negative_default_mode_towar.notes: Microsoft worked example: CEILING.MATH(-8.1,2) = -8 ('rounds -8.1 up (toward 0) to the nearest multiple of 2'). This is the modern, explicit-mode successor to legacy CEILING and was designed to match LibreOffice/ODF's CEILING(...,...,Mode) semantics for the default case.

CEILING.MATH_negative_mode_nonzero_away_.description: Negative number with a nonzero mode argument -> rounds away from zero instead of the toward-zero default.
CEILING.MATH_negative_mode_nonzero_away_.notes: Microsoft worked example: CEILING.MATH(-5.5,2,-1) = -6 ('rounds -5.5 down (away from 0) ... with a mode of -1'). Mode only affects negative numbers; any nonzero mode reverses the default direction.

CEILING_PRECISE_basic.description: Rounds up to the nearest multiple of 3

CEILING_PRECISE_already_multiple.description: A value already on a multiple is returned unchanged

CEILING_PRECISE_negative_rounds_up.description: Unlike CEILING, PRECISE always rounds toward positive infinity regardless of the significance sign, so -7 rounds up to -6

CELL_row_number.description: The documented "row" info_type returns the row number of the referenced cell
CELL_row_number.notes: Excel documents info_type "row" as returning the "Row number of the cell in reference". B7 is in row 7. This is one of the four info_types this corpus tests, because it depends only on the reference itself -- see the exclusions listed on the "type" cases below

CELL_column_number.description: The documented "col" info_type returns the column number of the referenced cell
CELL_column_number.notes: Excel documents info_type "col" as returning the "Column number of the cell in reference". Column D is the 4th column

CELL_column_of_range_uses_first_cell.description: A multi-cell reference, where the documentation says the upper-left cell is used
CELL_column_of_range_uses_first_cell.notes: Excel documents that "address" returns the "Reference of the first cell in reference" and that "contents" returns the "Value of the upper-left cell in reference", so a range argument resolves to its upper-left cell. C3 is in column C, the 3rd column

CELL_contents_of_number.description: The documented "contents" info_type returns the value of the referenced cell
CELL_contents_of_number.notes: Excel documents info_type "contents" as returning the "Value of the upper-left cell in reference; not a formula". A1 holds the number 42

CELL_type_value.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "v" for a cell holding a value
CELL_type_value.notes: Excel documents info_type "type" as returning "'v' for value if the cell contains anything else" (that is, anything other than blank or a text constant). A1 holds the number 42

CELL_type_label.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "l" for a cell holding a text constant
CELL_type_label.notes: Excel documents "type" as returning "'l' for label if the cell contains a text constant". A2 holds the text "hello"

CELL_type_blank.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "b" for an empty cell
CELL_type_blank.notes: Excel documents "type" as returning "'b' for blank if the cell is empty". A3 is deliberately left unset. EXCLUSIONS: this corpus tests only the four deterministic info_types "row", "col", "contents" and "type". The others are deliberately omitted because their results are not a property of the formula: "address" and "filename" depend on the workbook's path and quoting (and "filename" is documented to return empty text for an unsaved sheet); "format", "color", "parentheses", "prefix", "protect" and "width" depend on cell formatting, column width and sheet protection that survive an .xlsx round-trip inconsistently, and Microsoft documents all six as unsupported in Excel for the web, Excel Mobile and Excel Starter; and the reference-omitted form CELL(info_type) is excluded because Microsoft's own page warns it reports "your active cell" at calculation time and "does not reliably produce information about a specific cell" -- it is volatile by design and could not be asserted against any fixed value

CHAR_out_of_range_256.notes: Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/char-function-bbd249c8-b36e-4a91-8017-1c133f9b837a - valid range is 1-255; values outside it are invalid

CHIDIST_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: right-tailed chi-squared probability at x=18.307 with 10 degrees of freedom
CHIDIST_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.0500006. Independently derived from the documented definition CHIDIST = P(X > x) for a chi-squared random variable: scipy.stats.chi2.sf(18.307, 10) = 0.05000058909139812 -> 0.0500006 at 7 dp

CHIDIST_deg_freedom_truncated.description: A non-integer degrees-of-freedom argument, which the documentation says is truncated
CHIDIST_deg_freedom_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If deg_freedom is not an integer, it is truncated", so 10.9 must behave exactly as 10 and return the documented 0.0500006. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine 10.9 degrees of freedom would give chi2.sf(18.307, 10.9) = 0.071937

CHIDIST_one_degree_of_freedom.description: A second point on the distribution, at 1 degree of freedom
CHIDIST_one_degree_of_freedom.notes: Derived from the same documented right-tail definition: scipy.stats.chi2.sf(3, 1) = 0.08326451666355042 -> 0.0832645 at 7 dp. Equivalently 2*(1 - Phi(sqrt(3))), since a chi-squared variate with 1 degree of freedom is the square of a standard normal

CHIDIST_negative_x_num.notes: Excel documents: "If x is negative, CHIDIST returns the #NUM! error value."

CHIDIST_zero_deg_freedom_num.notes: Excel documents: "If deg_freedom < 1 or deg_freedom > 10^10, CHIDIST returns the #NUM! error value."

CHIDIST_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If either argument is nonnumeric, CHIDIST returns the #VALUE! error value."

CHIINV_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse of the right-tailed chi-squared probability 0.050001 at 10 degrees of freedom
CHIINV_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 18.306973. Independently derived from the documented definition CHIINV(p,df) = x such that CHIDIST(x,df) = p, i.e. the inverse survival function: scipy.stats.chi2.isf(0.050001, 10) = 18.30697345696106 -> 18.306973 at 6 dp. Cross-checked by round-trip: chi2.sf(18.30697345696106, 10) = 0.050001

CHIINV_second_point.description: A second point on the inverse: the median of the chi-squared distribution with 4 degrees of freedom
CHIINV_second_point.notes: Derived from the same documented inverse-survival definition: scipy.stats.chi2.isf(0.5, 4) = 3.3566939800333224 -> 3.35669398 at 8 dp. This point is not on Microsoft's page, so it tests the function against mathematics rather than against a published figure

CHIINV_deg_freedom_truncated.description: A non-integer degrees-of-freedom argument, which the documentation says is truncated
CHIINV_deg_freedom_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If deg_freedom is not an integer, it is truncated", so 10.9 must behave exactly as 10 and return the documented 18.306973. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine 10.9 degrees of freedom would give chi2.isf(0.050001, 10.9) = 19.539074

CHIINV_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If either argument is nonnumeric, CHIINV returns the #VALUE! error value."

CHISQ.DIST_doc_cumulative.description: Microsoft's first documented worked example: the cumulative chi-squared distribution at x=0.5 with 1 degree of freedom
CHISQ.DIST_doc_cumulative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.52049988. Independently derived from the documented cumulative form: scipy.stats.chi2.cdf(0.5, 1) = 0.5204998778130466 -> 0.52049988 at 8 dp. Equivalently 2*Phi(sqrt(0.5)) - 1, since a chi-squared variate with 1 degree of freedom is the square of a standard normal

CHISQ.DIST_doc_density.description: Microsoft's second documented worked example: the chi-squared probability density at x=2 with 3 degrees of freedom
CHISQ.DIST_doc_density.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.20755375. Independently derived from the documented density form: scipy.stats.chi2.pdf(2, 3) = 0.2075537487102974 -> 0.20755375 at 8 dp. Equivalently x^(df/2-1)*e^(-x/2) / (2^(df/2)*Gamma(df/2)) = sqrt(2)*e^(-1)/(2^1.5*Gamma(1.5))

CHISQ.DIST_deg_freedom_truncated.description: A non-integer degrees-of-freedom argument, which the documentation says is truncated
CHISQ.DIST_deg_freedom_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If deg_freedom is not an integer, it is truncated", so 3.7 must behave exactly as 3 and return the documented 0.20755375. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine 3.7 degrees of freedom would give chi2.pdf(2, 3.7) = 0.194519

CHISQ.INV_doc_example_1.description: Microsoft's first documented worked example: inverse of the left-tailed chi-squared probability 0.93 at 1 degree of freedom
CHISQ.INV_doc_example_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 3.283020286, which is a TRUNCATION rather than a rounding of the true value. Independently derived from the documented left-tail inverse: scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(0.93, 1) = 3.283020286759539, whose correct 9-decimal rounding is 3.283020287, not the published 3.283020286. Asserting at 8 dp (3.28302029) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the mathematically correct value agree, so this case tests the function rather than the page's truncation

CHISQ.INV_doc_example_2.description: Microsoft's second documented worked example: inverse of the left-tailed chi-squared probability 0.6 at 2 degrees of freedom
CHISQ.INV_doc_example_2.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 1.832581464. Independently derived two ways: scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(0.6, 2) = 1.83258146374831, and in closed form, since the chi-squared distribution with 2 degrees of freedom is exponential with mean 2, the inverse is -2*ln(1-0.6) = -2*ln(0.4) = 1.83258146374831 -> 1.832581464 at 9 dp
